codes.note: Five-digit form of the same size code

dimensions.note: Nominal size from the size code; Tesla publishes no datasheet for it. The five-digit form is 46800.

geometry.note: The commonly cited Tesla battery is tabless: current is collected over the end faces rather than through tabs.

variants.label: Teardown, Tesla 4680
variants.notes: Figures are from a teardown and test site, not a manufacturer datasheet: nominal voltage 3.7 V, mass 0.355 kg and nominal energy about 86.5 Wh. The reference table lists 23000 mAh. No cutoff, charge voltage or maximum current is published.

safety: Charge only with a charger made for lithium-ion batteries, using constant current then constant voltage (CC/CV) up to the charge voltage in the battery datasheet (4.2 V for cobalt, nickel and manganese chemistries, 3.65 V for lithium iron phosphate).
Do not discharge below the datasheet cutoff voltage (2.5 V for most batteries listed here); deep discharge damages the battery and a damaged battery should be discarded.
The metal can is the negative terminal. A torn or missing wrap exposes the can and can short the battery against a metal object or an adjacent battery.

Unprotected batteries have no overcharge, over-discharge or short-circuit protection of their own and need protection in the charger or the device; protected batteries carry a circuit board but should still be charged with a matching charger.

Transport limits apply: the U.S. FAA requires spare lithium-ion batteries to travel in carry-on baggage with the terminals protected against short circuit, and limits rechargeable lithium-ion batteries to 100 Wh each (FAA PackSafe).
Batteries of this size are used in vehicle packs and are not consumer replacement batteries.
history: Tesla introduced the 4680 concept in 2020; production began in 2023 (Wikipedia, List of battery sizes).
notes: Size code: 46 mm diameter, 80 mm length, 0 for cylindrical; the five-digit form is 46800.
